questions.q: According to the lesson, what are the three buckets AI governance is organized around?
options: The data going in, the model itself, and the decisions coming out
Marketing, sales, and finance
Hardware, software, and networking
Hiring, training, and firing
questions.explain: The lesson organizes AI governance — and much of this course — around data in, the model, and decisions out.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what carries forward unchanged from existing data governance into AI governance?
options: Data owners and stewards still own the datasets feeding a model, and existing quality dimensions still define good data
Nothing — every role and standard must be rebuilt from scratch for AI
Only the company's logo and branding
The requirement that all data must be deleted before training a model
questions.explain: The lesson states that data-side roles and the quality dimensions carry forward and get extended, not replaced.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how can an AI system create privacy risk without a traditional data breach?
options: The model itself can memorize and reproduce pieces of training data, or combine outputs in a way that re-identifies someone
Privacy risk only ever happens through a stolen laptop
AI systems are incapable of handling personal data in any form
Privacy risk requires a government investigation to exist at all
questions.explain: The lesson explains that memorization and re-identification through outputs mean the model itself can become the exposure.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what fundamentally distinguishes a machine learning model from traditional software?
options: Its behavior is learned statistically from data rather than written as explicit rules by a person
It runs on a different kind of computer hardware
It cannot be deployed over the internet
It always requires more storage space than any traditional program
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that a model's logic is learned from data, not authored as explicit, readable rules.

questions.q: What is the one governance requirement the lesson says is genuinely new for synthetic data, compared to real data?
options: Clear documentation that the data is synthetic, rather than blended invisibly into "the training data"
A requirement that synthetic data never be used in any model
A requirement that synthetic data be deleted immediately after generation
A requirement that only government agencies may generate synthetic data
questions.explain: The lesson names documentation honesty — disclosing that data is synthetic — as the one requirement without a direct equivalent for real data.

questions.q: In supervised learning, as described in the lesson, what is a label?
options: The correct-answer tag paired with an example that the model learns to predict
The file name given to a dataset before upload
A physical sticker placed on server hardware
The version number of the model's training code
questions.explain: The lesson defines a label as the correct-answer tag paired with training examples, which the model learns to predict for new data.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say training data needs governance beyond what a general data governance program already provides?
options: Its patterns get absorbed into a model's parameters and applied to every future prediction, unlike a report that gets corrected when caught
Training data is never stored in any system, so no policy can apply to it
Training data is always smaller in volume than other data
Machine learning models do not actually use data from an organization
questions.explain: The lesson's key point is that training data's influence persists in the model until retraining, unlike a report that gets corrected on the spot.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what changes about the six quality dimensions (accuracy, completeness, consistency, validity, uniqueness, timeliness) when applied to training data instead of a report?
options: The consequence of failing them — a training data flaw gets learned as a pattern and applied automatically, without human judgment
The dimensions themselves are completely replaced with new ones for machine learning
The dimensions no longer matter at all once data is used to train a model
Training data is exempt from quality standards entirely
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that the same six dimensions still apply — what changes is the severity of the consequence when they fail.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say it doesn't matter which specific registry tool (MLflow, Azure ML, SageMaker, Vertex AI) a team uses?
options: What matters for governance is that registering a model is the only supported path to production, regardless of tool
Because none of these tools actually track model versions
Because only one of these tools is a real product
Because governance doesn't apply to machine learning models
questions.explain: The governance requirement is behavioral — registration as the only path to production — not tied to any single vendor's implementation.

questions.q: What are the five typical approval gates the lesson describes, in order?
options: Development, technical validation, risk/compliance review, business sign-off, production approval
Marketing, sales, legal, finance, HR
Training, testing, deployment, monitoring, retirement only, with no sign-offs
A single gate: whether the model's accuracy is above 90%
questions.explain: The lesson lists these five gates explicitly, each checking something different before a version can be promoted.

questions.q: What is 'impact analysis,' as the lesson defines it?
options: Using lineage to determine which models and decisions were affected after a data problem is discovered
A financial report on a model's return on investment
A survey sent to end users after a product launch
The process of choosing which model to deploy first
questions.explain: Impact analysis is explicitly defined as using lineage to find every downstream model and decision affected once an upstream data problem surfaces.

questions.q: Who does a well-written model card need to serve, according to the lesson?
options: Both technical builders/reviewers and non-technical stakeholders like compliance officers or regulators
Only the original author of the model, for their own reference
Only external auditors, never internal engineers
Only end users of the application, never engineers
questions.explain: A card that serves only one audience is incomplete — it needs both the technical detail builders need and the plain-language framing non-technical reviewers need.

questions.q: What access does a customer-facing application calling a model for predictions actually need, per the lesson's least-privilege example?
options: Inference access only — no business touching training data or the raw model file
Full administrative access to the model registry
Direct read access to the raw training data
Write access to retrain the model on demand
questions.explain: The lesson specifies inference-only access for this role — anything beyond that is over-granting.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what has to be decided before a model ships, not improvised after an alert fires?
options: Who is on call for the model's alerts and what actions they're authorized to take, such as rollback or escalation
The exact wording of the model's marketing description
The model's final accuracy score, which can be decided at any time
Whether the company will ever build another model
questions.explain: The lesson stresses that an on-call owner and authorized response actions must be defined in advance, or an alert is just an unread log entry.

questions.q: How does the lesson define 'hallucination'?
options: A confident, fluent model output that isn't actually supported by any real, verifiable source
A model crashing and producing no output at all
A deliberate test conducted by the security team
An output that is always obviously and visibly wrong
questions.explain: The lesson specifically notes hallucinated output is dangerous because it looks just as authoritative as a correct answer — not because it's obviously wrong.

questions.q: Why is Python's pickle format called out as a real, specific security risk for model files?
options: Because loading a pickle file executes arbitrary code embedded in it, so a malicious file can run anything on the machine that loads it
Because pickle files are always larger than other formats
Because pickle is incompatible with all machine learning frameworks
Because pickle files cannot be version-controlled
questions.explain: This is the lesson's real, documented example: pickle's deserialization executes code, which is a genuine, well-known security issue with the format.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why does AI risk management ask a harder question than traditional IT risk management?
options: Because a system working exactly as designed can still produce an unfair or unsafe outcome at scale, with no outage to alert anyone
Because AI systems never have outages
Because traditional IT risk management doesn't consider reputational damage
Because AI systems are always more expensive to build
questions.explain: The lesson's key point is that AI risk can hide inside normal, working-as-designed operation, unlike an outage that triggers an alert.

questions.q: In the lesson's five-step audit structure, what comes right after scoping which systems are in the audit?
options: Requesting the evidence items by name before the audit begins
Immediately firing the system's owner
Publishing the findings to the public before review
Skipping straight to remediation with no evidence review
questions.explain: The five steps are scope, evidence request, walkthrough, gap identification, and findings/remediation, in that order.

questions.q: What is this lesson's own explicit framing of its content?
options: Orientation, not legal advice — any real compliance decision needs a qualified professional and the current primary text
A complete, authoritative legal compliance checklist
A guarantee that following it makes an organization compliant
A substitute for consulting a lawyer in any jurisdiction
questions.explain: The lesson repeats, deliberately, that it is orientation only and not a basis for a real compliance decision.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what does the accountability principle require?
options: A specific person or role owns the system's behavior and outcomes — "the model did it" is not an acceptable answer
Every employee must personally review every model decision
The vendor who built the model is always legally responsible
No AI system can ever be deployed without unanimous board approval
questions.explain: Accountability means a named owner is responsible for the system's behavior, not that everyone or no one is responsible.

questions.q: How did the team score the chatbot's risk tier compared to Harrow Peak's credit model, and why?
options: Lower overall, since impact was more recoverable, but still high enough to require active monitoring rather than a launch-and-forget approach
Identical in every respect to the credit model's risk tier
Zero risk, since chatbots can never cause real harm
Higher than the credit model, because chatbots are always riskier than scoring models
questions.explain: The lesson describes the chatbot's tier as lower than the credit model's (more recoverable impact) but still requiring active monitoring.

questions.q: What course does the lesson name as the next step in the Data Governance career path?
options: Data Governance Program Management
Advanced Python for Data Science
Salesforce Administration
Kafka and Event Streaming
questions.explain: The lesson's closing section names Data Governance Program Management as the next course in the path, applying this course's sequencing to the whole data estate.

questions.q: What is Harrow Peak Financial, as presented in this lesson?
options: A fictional company invented for this course's illustrative case study, not a real organization or incident
A real regional bank whose incident was reported in the news
A real fintech startup mentioned in the EU AI Act
An anonymized version of a real lawsuit
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly labels Harrow Peak Financial as fictional and illustrative, not a real company or incident.
